climbing_route.label: Lower south face
climbing_route.notes: Solid 3rd- and 4th-class scrambling on the lower face, reached by a short climb/traverse from a glacier-side camp toward the base of the peak. No technical rock gear is required for the standard line.

climbing_route.label: Upper broken face
climbing_route.notes: Transitions to looser, more broken 3rd-class rock higher up — take care with rockfall onto anyone below. Expect the climbing to run longer than the peak's modest height suggests since the face is broader than it looks from the glacier; a rope is worth carrying in case conditions call for a belay on the looser upper section.

wa_tomyhoi_peak_southeast_ridge.skip_reason: The approach text stops at the base of the summit block — it explicitly measures the approach as ~6-7 miles from the trailhead to that point and describes nothing above it. The loose, exposed sidehilling on scree and rock benches, the Tomyhoi Glacier top-edge traverse and the notch/moat at ~7,250 ft below the false summit are all stated as approach terrain.

climbing_route.label: Icy-Spruce Pass to the south ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: From high camp the climb proper begins by crossing Icy-Spruce Pass and making a rising traverse over snow, talus, and rock slabs to reach the crest of Agnes' south ridge just south of Point 7760. The standard line follows Asa Peak's northeast ridge onto Agnes' south ridge.

climbing_route.label: South ridge
climbing_route.notes: Roped Class 4-5 rock leads up the ridge; the roped class 4-5 pitches begin once the standard line gains Agnes' south ridge.

climbing_route.label: West col to 8,200 ft on the west ridge
climbing_route.notes: From camp climb NNE to the broad col on the west side of Cashmere Mountain (~8,000 ft), then follow the west ridge itself up to about 8,200 ft. The class 3-4 scrambling begins near the col and continues to the summit on loose, blocky rock with some exposure.

climbing_route.label: Gendarmed upper ridge
climbing_route.notes: The upper ridge is a series of tooth-like gendarmes separated by roughly five main notches, and the route weaves back and forth between the north and south sides of the crest rather than following it directly — expect real route-finding.

climbing_route.label: Traverse to the northwest gully
climbing_route.notes: Make a rising traverse/contour several hundred yards around to the northwest side of the summit pyramid to a northwest-facing gully; this gully leads to the summit.

climbing_route.label: North face to the summit
climbing_route.notes: From the notch between Chianti and Burgundy Spires — gained via a rappel from the west side per the original account, or by traversing in from Burgundy Col — climb the north face directly to the summit.

climbing_route.label: Southeast ridge to the notch
climbing_route.notes: From the ridge, gained at about 7,000 ft, work climber's-left up ledges and short rock steps toward a notch at roughly 7,900-7,920 ft just east of the summit block. The east face sheds rock, especially as the day warms, so a helmet is worth carrying; snow can linger across the traverse well into July, so an axe (and possibly crampons) is worth having for early-season attempts.

climbing_route.label: Summit block finish
climbing_route.notes: Finish through blocky class 3 terrain to the 8,107 ft summit; some parties rope up for a few class 4 moves near the top.

climbing_route.label: Open ridge above Fish Creek Pass
climbing_route.notes: From the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up the obvious boot path/climbers' trail that switchbacks northwest up the open ridge toward Courtney Peak, gaining roughly 900-1,000 ft on easy class 2 tundra and talus with a good game/climbers' path most of the way.

climbing_route.label: Upper boulders to the summit block
climbing_route.notes: A few hundred feet below the summit it steepens into larger class 2+ boulders that require careful hopping and some route-finding to the summit block. Snow can linger in the gullies near the pass and on the upper ridge into July, so an ice axe is worth carrying for early-season (June) attempts.

climbing_route.label: Southwest ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: From Earl Pass, leave the trail and pick up the boot path climbing the southwest ridge directly toward the summit. This final ~800 vertical feet is the crux of the trip: a sustained, unrelenting class 2 scramble on loose scree, sand, and broken rock with only an intermittent climbers' track — go slow, test holds, and be mindful of kicking rock onto anyone below. The ridge tops out on Earl Peak's 7,036-ft summit.
